analysis.one_liner: Redirects part of Social Security payroll taxes into personal investment accounts while trimming traditional benefits and raising the retirement age.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 1999 with bipartisan sponsorship and referred to the Ways and Means Social Security Subcommittee, but it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created an "Individual Security Account" for every worker born after 1944, funded by redirecting a portion of Social Security payroll taxes (reducing the employee share from 6.2% to 4.2% plus a 2% account contribution) and by optional extra deposits that the government would match. Workers' traditional Social Security checks would have been reduced, and the bill cut benefits in several other ways: raising the normal retirement age further, raising the early-retirement penalty, counting more low-earning years in the benefit formula, and slowing the annual inflation adjustment used to compute cost-of-living increases. It also added a new minimum benefit for the lowest earners, eliminated the earnings test for beneficiaries past retirement age, and required transfers from the general Treasury fund to the Social Security trust fund.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, workers born after 1944 would have gained personal accounts holding a portion of their payroll taxes, with government matching contributions (50% match up to limits, including on EITC dollars) and tax-free growth inside the accounts. The lowest earners would have gained a new minimum Social Security benefit, and older beneficiaries who work would have gained from repeal of the earnings test. The financial industry would also have gained a vast new stream of assets to manage, since every worker's payroll diversion would flow into investment funds.

how_it_helps.text: It would have created an Individual Security Account for every worker born after 1944, funded by a redirection of a share of payroll taxes plus voluntary contributions, invested like the federal Thrift Savings Plan.

It provided a 50% government match (up to limits) on voluntary contributions and allowed Earned Income Tax Credit amounts to be deposited into the accounts, giving low-income workers a savings vehicle and match they otherwise rarely have.

It established a new minimum monthly Social Security benefit (60% of the poverty-line level, phased in after 2005 for beneficiaries with at least 20 years of work) and eliminated the earnings test that reduces benefits for beneficiaries past retirement age who keep working.

It directed Treasury general-fund transfers into the Social Security trust fund and set up a mechanism for the Trustees and President to propose fixes if trust fund balances were projected to fall to zero.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would have fallen on future Social Security beneficiaries through slower cost-of-living increases, higher retirement ages, steeper early-retirement penalties, a longer benefit-averaging period, and reduced benefit formula factors — with the traditional benefit cut most for higher earners. Taxpayers generally would bear the general-fund transfers to the trust fund. Workers would also bear investment risk on the individual-account portion of their retirement income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Future Social Security beneficiaries and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill phased in a higher full retirement age (rising beyond 67), a higher early-retirement age, a higher early-retirement penalty, and longer averaging of earnings in the benefit formula — each of which cuts lifetime benefits, hitting workers in physically demanding jobs and lower earners hardest.

Section 8 redefines the cost-of-living adjustment by subtracting an estimate of CPI 'substitution bias' from annual increases, which would compound over time and reduce benefits not just for Social Security but also for civil service, military retirement, railroad retirement, and federal workers' compensation COLAs — a slow, permanent benefit cut.

Workers would pay the same or nearly the same payroll tax while their traditional defined benefit would be reduced to fund the new accounts, shifting investment risk in retirement income from the pooled government program onto individual households; the minimum-benefit floor would not begin until 2006 and would not be indexed to wage growth.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real problem — Social Security's long-run shortfall — and included genuinely progressive pieces, notably a higher minimum benefit and the option for low-income workers to build savings through EITC deposits. But the core trade it offered was steep: workers would surrender roughly a third of their promised Social Security benefit to fund the accounts, take on market risk in retirement, and face slower benefit growth from a changed inflation measure, while any new individual accounts would channel contributions into the private financial industry. Critics would also note that diverting payroll taxes from the trust fund deepens the near-term funding gap the bill claims to close, requiring the general fund transfers and formula cuts it builds in. On balance, the bill's design placed much of the risk and the cost of solvency on ordinary workers' benefits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security Subcommittee in May 1999 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote; it died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Kolbe introduced H.R. 1793 on May 13, 1999, joined by Reps. Stenholm, Smith of Michigan, Dooley, Sanford, McCarthy of Missouri, and Greenwood as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and the Rules Committee on the day of introduction, and on May 20, 1999 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Social Security.
The bill attracted 11 cosponsors, split evenly between five Democrats and six Republicans.

No further action was recorded after the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 10, 1999; the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote and died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one can be said to have gained from the outcome itself. The traditional Social Security benefit structure, including its cost-of-living formula and retirement ages, remained unchanged, which beneficiaries of the current program are better off with; the financial industry likewise gained nothing because no individual accounts were created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Traditional Social Security as it stood

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 13, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks on June 10, 1999.

for.name: House Ways and Means Committee / Subcommittee on Social Security
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and the Social Security Subcommittee took no recorded action on it; no hearing or markup is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 11 cosponsors split five Democrats and six Republicans, with original cosponsors from both parties — and there is no record of opposition, since the bill never advanced to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have routed a share of every worker's payroll tax into individual investment accounts modeled on the Thrift Savings Plan, creating a large new pool of managed assets. Because it never advanced, the industry gained nothing from it.

For beneficiaries, the bill would have slowed COLAs via a revised CPI measure and cut benefits through formula and retirement-age changes, while offering a higher minimum benefit for the lowest earners. For workers, it traded part of the guaranteed benefit for individual accounts.
